slides.title: Hyperliquid in Five Minutes
slides.subtitle:
An L1 where the order book is part of consensus
Ryan Sauge - v1.0 - 2026-10-01
slides.notes: Source: The Hyperliquid Protocol - HyperCore, HyperEVM and Onchain Perpetual Mechanics (https://rya-sge.github.io/access-denied/2026/09/02/hyperliquid-protocol-architecture/) and the Hyperliquid documentation. Talk length: about 5 minutes.

slides.title: What is Hyperliquid
bullets: A DEX for perpetual futures and spot, on its own chain
Many DEXs keep the book off-chain, or use an AMM
Here, order book, margin and liquidations are onchain state
Question: what if the exchange is the chain itself?
slides.notes: (25 s) Most people know Hyperliquid as a perp exchange. The design choice behind it is that the matching engine is not an app deployed on a chain. Every validator runs it.

slides.title: Architecture: one consensus
bullets: HyperBFT: a block is final with 2/3 of staked HYPE
HyperCore: order books, clearinghouses, oracle, staking
HyperEVM: a regular EVM, chain ID 999
Same consensus, no bridge between the two
slides.notes: (30 s) For a co-located client, the median time from sending an order to a committed answer is 0.2 seconds. Mainnet handles about 200 000 orders per second, and the documentation says execution is the bottleneck, not consensus.

slides.title: The life of an order
bullets: Inside a block, actions run in three groups:
Orders that take no liquidity (post-only)
Cancels
Orders that take liquidity (GTC, IOC)
Margin is checked at placement and again at each match
slides.notes: (35 s) A market maker who cancels and a trader who hits the same quote in the same block: the cancel wins. That removes a form of front-running that a first-come, first-served block allows. Margin is checked when the order is placed, and again for the resting order at each match, because the price may have moved between the two.

slides.title: Prices: oracle and mark
bullets: Oracle: two medians, every ~3 s, used for funding
Mark: median of 3 indices, used for margin and liquidation
slides.notes: (30 s) One consequence: a position can be liquidated with no trade on Hyperliquid at that price, because the mark price also reads external markets. The oracle has its own deck if someone wants the details.

slides.title: Liquidation: on the order book
bullets: Anyone can take the other side of the liquidation orders
Above 100 000 USDC: 20% at a time, then a 30 s cooldown
slides.notes: (20 s) Maintenance margin is half the initial margin at maximum leverage, so between 1.25% and 16.7% depending on the asset. Most liquidations end at this step.

slides.title: Liquidation: backstop and ADL
bullets: Auto-deleveraging (ADL) closes the most profitable, most levered opposite positions first
A user with no open position never pays for platform losses
slides.notes: (20 s) The trader does not get the maintenance margin back at step 2: HLP keeps it so that backstop liquidations are profitable on average.

slides.title: HyperEVM and HyperCore
bullets: Read: values match HyperCore when the EVM block was built
Write: CoreWriter orders are delayed by a few seconds
Small blocks every second (3M gas)
Big blocks every minute (30M gas)
slides.notes: (30 s) This is how a lending protocol or a vault on the HyperEVM can trade on the order book and price its collateral with the same number the clearinghouse uses.

slides.title: The HIP standards
table: Standard
What it adds
HIP-1
Anyone can deploy a token and its spot market (Dutch auction, 500 HYPE floor)
HIP-2
Hyperliquidity: onchain market making, 0.3% spread refreshed every 3 s
HIP-3
Anyone can run a perp exchange; the deployer publishes the oracle, 500 000 HYPE staked
HIP-4
Fully collateralised outcome markets, no leverage, e.g. prediction markets
slides.notes: (30 s) Green: spot tokens and their liquidity. Blue: new market types, perps and outcomes. HIP-2 attaches to a HIP-1 token at deployment, which is why those two are linked.

slides.title: Where the fees go
bullets: Base perp fees: 0.045% taker, 0.015% maker
Staking HYPE: up to 40% off
No operator cut; HLP also runs backstop liquidations
Staking rewards: ~2.37%/year at 400M HYPE staked
slides.notes: (25 s) HLP is the vault from slide 6. Anyone can deposit into it, with a four-day lock-up after each deposit.

slides.title: Limitations
table: Limitation (by design)
What it means for a user
2/3 of the stake can change any state
Order book, oracle and votes share one trust assumption
Validator votes decide offchain questions
Delistings, HIP-3 slashing, quote assets: judgement by stake
HIP-3 oracle is one deployer
Slashed stake is burned; users are not compensated
HyperEVM token links are not verified
A linked contract can hold arbitrary code
No automatic slashing of validators
Misbehaving validators are jailed by vote
slides.notes: (30 s) None of this is hidden; the documentation states each point. The trust model reduces to how HYPE stake is distributed across validators.

slides.title: Conclusion
bullets: On Hyperliquid, the exchange is the chain's state machine
Cancels before takers, margin checked at each match, fixed liquidation steps
The cost: one trust assumption, two thirds of the staked HYPE
slides.notes: (25 s) Back to the opening question. An exchange that is the chain gets a central-exchange order book with onchain settlement, and puts all its trust in the validator set.
